newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's parliament bans Western terms.
newsitem.headline: Iran's parliament bans Western terms.

text.p: Iran's parliament on Wednesday approved a law that bans both the government and private sector from using Western terms in reports and speeches and halts their use on consumer goods.

Alarmed by growing signs of Western cultural influences in Iran, especially among youth, the law seeks to crack down on producers and distributors of products decorated with Western alphabets and symbols.
The legislation also prohibits the use of Western terms by both the government and the private sector in speeches, correspondence, reports and interviews.
The punishment for violators ranges from warnings to the withdrawal of work permits. Police are authorised to remove signs and merchandise from stores displaying foreign alphabets.
Parliament said the ban served "to preserve the strength of the Farsi (Iranian) language, one of the pillars of Iran's national identity".
The law calls on Iran's Academy of Culture and Language to "coin or choose Farsi equivalants for foreign terms".
The legislation exempts terms for which the academy has not yet found equivalants or does not deem alternatives necessary.
The parliamentary debate was broadcast live on Tehran radio.

Deputy Abbas Abbasi complained about the tendency of "some families to choose foreign names for their children". Tehran residents say names like Sonia and Patricia are no longer uncommon in the capital.
Another parliamentarian criticised the Western linguistic influence on consumer goods.
"One of the biggest inroads of the Western cultural invasion takes the form of signs and symbols on children's clothes, bags and shoes," Mohammad Madahi said.
Markets in the Islamic republic are filled with shirts, sweaters and knapsacks adorned with big capital letters from the Latin alphabet, as well as names such as Sony, Popeye, Walt Disney and Paris.
The legislation grants a two-year grace period for product names and one year for company names to eliminate any foreign influence.

The legislation still requires final approval from the Guardian Council, a body of six attorneys and six clerics who check the bill against Islamic Sharia law and the constitution for any inconsistencies.
